title: Nate Bargatze Sets Guinness World Record for Most Tickets Sold for a Stand-Up Comedy Tour (EXCLUSIVE)
description:
Nate Bargatze and his “Big Dumb Eyes” just set a Guinness World Record.

	The Tennessee-born comedian has officially sold the most tickets for a sta
body:
Nate Bargatze and his “Big Dumb Eyes” just set a Guinness World Record.

	The Tennessee-born comedian has officially sold the most tickets for a stand-up comedy tour, surpassing the previously record held by Jeff Dunham.

	Bargatze will be presented with the Guinness World Record onstage at the Scotiabank Arena in Toronto on Saturday. Ahead of the show, his “Big Dumb Eyes” world tour had sold approximately 2,016,254 tickets, passing Dunham’s “Spark of Insanity” tour, which sold 1,981,720 tickets. The final ticket number on Bargatze’s Guinness World Records certificate will be confirmed later this weekend.
	

	Bargatze accomplished the feat at an impressive pace. To achieve the previous record, Dunham sold 1,981,720 tickets across 386 venues between Sept. 13, 2007, and Aug. 21, 2010 (35 months and 8 days). Bargatze’s “Big Dumb Eyes” tour, which began on April 6, 2025, crossed the 2 million mark after just 16 months and 10 days — and across only 128 venues. (There were also no puppets on the Bargatze tour.)


	Along the way, Bargatze broke 84 venue records, according to his reps, which included becoming the only comedian to sell out three consecutive performances at Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena in a single calendar year — a feat matched only by Taylor Swift and Garth Brooks.

	Bargatze, whose clean, deadpan comedy has made him famous among all age groups, was crowned by Pollstar as the highest-grossing stand-up comic, with $77.5 million reported in 2025 alone. Earlier this year, he crossed over onto the silver screen with his movie “The Breadwinner,” and he is currently planning to build a $350 million theme park in his home state of Tennessee called Nateland.
	

	Bargatze is repped by Brillstein Entertainment Partners, UTA, Ginsburg Daniels Kallis and 2PM Sharp.

schema.headline: Nate Bargatze Sets Guinness World Record for Most Tickets Sold for a Stand-Up Comedy Tour (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Box Office: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Chomps on $8.1 Million, But ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is Still No. 1 With $19 Million
description:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” led the box office again on Friday despite competition from Anne Hathaway and a horde of hungry dinosaurs.

	The Warner
body:
“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” led the box office again on Friday despite competition from Anne Hathaway and a horde of hungry dinosaurs.

	The Warner Bros. sci-fi thriller “The End of Oak Street” landed in second place on opening day with $8.1 million from 3,446 North American theaters. Rivals estimate the film will earn about $18.7 million domestically by Sunday. That’s a soft start since “Oak Street” cost more than $80 million to produce. Reviews (84% on Rotten Tomatoes) and word-of-mouth (”B” grade on CinemaScore exit polls) have been positive, so there is a chance “Oak Street” sticks around in theaters and justifies its price tag.
	

	“It Follows” filmmaker David Robert Mitchell wrote and directed “The End of Oak Street,” which chronicles a suburban family whose neighborhood is suddenly blipped to prehistoric times. Hathaway stars alongside Ewan McGregor, Maisy Stella, Christian Convery and Jordan Alexa Davis.


	This weekend’s other major newcomer, “PAW Patrol: The Dino Movie,” took third after earning $7.35 million on Friday from 3,545 North American cinemas. The animated family adventure should dig up about $20 million for Paramount through the weekend. That projection aligns with its predecessor, “The Mighty Movie,” which opened with $22 million and grossed $205 million by the end of its run.

	“Spider-Man: Brand New Day” still reigned supreme with $19 million domestically on Friday. Through its third weekend, the Marvel-Sony tentpole is targeting $67 million, which represents about a 53% decline from last week’s numbers. That would push “Brand New Day’s” North American revenues to roughly $783 million.
	

	Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is still holding strong at No. 4 through its fifth weekend. The Greek epic added $6.5 million domestically on Friday and is expected to pull in $23 million through the weekend. That would put the film’s North American haul at $504 million.

	Finally, in fifth was “Katseye: Wild Hearts.” The documentary, which offers a behind-the-scenes look at the global girl group, made an estimated $2.2 million on Friday from just 724 theaters. By Sunday, it’s expected to gross about $3.8 million.

schema.headline: Box Office: ‘The End of Oak Street’ Chomps on $8.1 Million, But ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is Still No. 1 With $19 Million

title: Darren Walker Opens His Home to Friends and Anonymous Content Emmy Nominees in Celebration of ‘Joy, Reflection, Delight and Awe’
description: Darren Walker may be new to Los Angeles as he takes the helm of Anonymous Content as president and CEO, but he’s had long relationships with key pla
body:
Darren Walker may be new to Los Angeles as he takes the helm of Anonymous Content as president and CEO, but he’s had long relationships with key players in town for years, given his distinguished career in philanthropy and nonprofits. 

	Sally Field is one of those people. So Walker was excited to learn when he took the role at Anonymous Content at the start of this year that Field was a client. And Field was there on Wednesday evening to cheer on her friend as Walker toasted Anonymous Content’s Emmy nominees this year and showed off his famous new digs at a historic Los Angeles address.
	

	Walker delighted the intimate crowd of a few dozen friends and associates with the kismet story of how he came to purchase the sui generis, 4,400-square foot property designed as the personal residence of legendary Los Angeles architect Paul Revere Williams. 


	Much of the home is outfitted with original fixtures and an array of bespoke touches that the renowned architect handcrafted for his family residence. The home is in a historic neighborhood that reflected post-World War II Los Angeles’ embrace of mid-century modern building design and mid-century, West Coast modern attitudes about race, class and equality. 

	Of all the intricate and meticulously designed touches that Walker pointed out in the home, the one that generated the most oohs and ahhs was the lovingly built, extra-large vanity that Williams built into one wall for his wife, Della Mae Williams. At one point it was complete with giant, helmet-style hair dryers and salon-style chairs, but sadly those were gutted by a previous owner, Walker explained. Della Mae’s home beauty salon — big enough for her to invite a few friends — was but one example of how Williams was determined to present his wife with “every one of the beautiful luxuries that he built into the homes of the wealthiest families in Beverly Hills and Brentwood,” Walker said.
	



	

					Emmy nominees Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn, Sally Field, Sarah Pidgeon and Sonja Warfield flank Anonymous Content chief Darren Walker at the Anonymous Content Emmy Party held Aug. 12 at Walker’s home in Los Angeles. (Todd Williamson / JanuaryImages)
									Todd Williamson/JanuaryImages for Anonymous Content
	



	Walker’s rise to national prominence and influence in philanthropy during his run atop of the Ford Foundation mirrors Williams’ ascent in his field. Walker made the 90-degree turn to lead a talent management firm active in content development came at the behest of his longtime friend Laurene Powell Jobs, whose Emerson Collective owns Anonymous Content. 

	Walker’s enthusiasm for his new job was evident in his neatly arranged, oh-so-classic Mid-City Los Angeles backyard as he introduced Anonymous Content’s Emmy nominees in attendance one by one: Sally Field (for her star turn in the Netflix film “Remarkably Bright Creatures”; Kate O’Flynn (“Widow’s Bay”), Sarah Pidgeon (“Love Story: John F Kennedy Jr. and Carolyn Bessette,”) Matthew Rhys (“The Beast in Me,” “Widow’s Bay”), Sonja Warfield (“The Gilded Age”).

	“I’m delighted to welcome you to this celebration at a time when we need moments for inspiration and joy, reflection, delight and awe and to recognize excellence more than ever,” Walker told the crowd. 

	Among those lending an ear and munching on light appetizers were Ava DuVernay, Thomas Doherty, Andy Parker, Kal Penn, Rich Appel, Keith Cox, Dee Johnson, Sophie de Bruijn, Jeremy Barber, Jiao Chen, Michael Dinner, LACMA’s Michael Govan, Jeff Sharp, Dan Lin, Kevin McCormick, Courtenay Miles, Lisa Taback, Matt Tyrnauer, Bryan Unkeless and Talitha Watkins.

	(Pictured top: Darren Walker with Emmy nominee Sarah Pidgeon)

schema.headline: Darren Walker Opens His Home to Friends and Anonymous Content Emmy Nominees in Celebration of ‘Joy, Reflection, Delight and Awe’

title: ‘Frozen 3’ First Details: Anna and Kristoff Get Married, Olaf Gets a Girlfriend and a New Villain Emerges
description:
Thanksgiving 2027 is about to get a lot colder. 

	Disney has revealed the first details about “Frozen 3,” which will release in theaters Nov. 24, 2
body:
Thanksgiving 2027 is about to get a lot colder. 

	Disney has revealed the first details about “Frozen 3,” which will release in theaters Nov. 24, 2027, following the previous two films’ tradition of Thanksgiving-centered premiere dates.

	Set in the fictional land of Arendelle, the cast of voice actors includes Kristen Bell as Anna, Idina Menzel as Elsa, Jonathan Groff as Kristoff and Josh Gad as Olaf. 


	The plot is being kept hush-hush, but we now know that Anna and Kristoff get married, a new villain is introduced and Olaf is getting a love interest named Samantha.
	

	Disney revealed the concept art for “Frozen 3″ by Britney Lee back in August 2024, which showed Elsa on a white horse and Anna on a brown stag.

	Bell previously told Variety in October 2025 that production was getting underway, though she hadn’t heard any of the film’s music at that point. The actress also denied reports she’ll earn $60 million to reprise her role as Princess Anna, though she didn’t disclose how much she’ll be paid.

	Former Disney CEO Bob Iger had also revealed that a fourth installment of “Frozen” is already in the works, though no further information has been released. Husband-and-wife duo Kristen Anderson-Lopez and Robert Lopez will compose the music for the two upcoming projects after serving as songwriters for the first two films.

	The first “Frozen” premiered in 2013 and was co-directed by Chris Buck and Jennifer Lee, who also wrote the film. Inspired by “The Snow Queen” by Hans Christian Andersen, “Frozen” went on to earn $1.3 billion worldwide and won two Oscars, including Best Animated Feature. Buck and Lee returned to helm the 2019 sequel, which brought in $1.45 billion.

schema.headline: ‘Frozen 3’ First Details: Anna and Kristoff Get Married, Olaf Gets a Girlfriend and a New Villain Emerges

title: Urša Menart Recalls Finding Inspiration on Influencers’ Fake Tragic Life Stories for Intimate Dramedy ‘Everything That’s Wrong With You’
description: Right before the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the world, Slovenian director Urša Menart came across a curious phenomenon on the internet: young peopl
body:
Right before the COVID-19 pandemic shut down the world, Slovenian director Urša Menart came across a curious phenomenon on the internet: young people, mostly women, making up tragic life stories to gather the increasingly sparse attention span of their followers. Even more curiously, the director realized people would often drop everything to visit these micro-influencers. The muddled parasocial relationship between poster and follower would come to inspire “Everything That’s Wrong With You,” having its world premiere as part of the narrative feature competition section at this year’s Sarajevo Film Festival. 
	

	The dramedy first finds young Maruša (Anuša Kodelja) back in her home country of Slovenia after a season living in Berlin. She just lost her mother to cancer, and the grief only amplifies her sense of displacement. While aimlessly scrolling one day, Maruša comes across Alja (Klara Kuk), a nurse living in a small coastal town in Germany. She sends a first message, which quickly spirals into a fast-developing friendship that is put to the test once they finally meet in person. 


	“What fascinated me wasn’t really the aspect of people inventing these stories, but the other side, those who befriended those folks, who followed them, who traveled across continents to visit them,” Menart tells Variety. “This was the first germ of the idea, but then the whole isolation of COVID and becoming a mother for the first time made me super lonely at times. It got me thinking about the human need to connect.”

	The two main characters were born out of the director’s observations and “interesting people” she met and read about. In the almost seven years it took to get the project off the ground, Menart worked on other films such as “My Last Year as a Loser,” but continued to think about the story and work on research. 
	

	“In Slovenia, the production process is quite long,” she notes. “It takes a while even after getting financing to secure co-producers, financing from abroad and so on. I always worried: will this theme even interest me six years from now? Because making a film is a marathon.”

	Little could Menart know that the themes of her film would only become more relevant in the years since, especially as the rapid advancement of technologies such as artificial intelligence amplified conversations around loneliness and the need for human connection. “Humans are connecting more and more with machines, while on the other hand slowly realizing how important it is to spend actual time with each other.”



	

					Urša Menart, courtesy of Rado Likon
	



	As major discussions around the male loneliness epidemic and how young men are being seduced into the dark corners of the manosphere and red-pill movements due to an increase in isolation, Menart offers a careful observation on how loneliness affects young women. “Everything That’s Wrong With You” broaches questions on the burden of caring, the pressures of coupling up and bearing children and the hypersexualized universe of online dating. 

	“I’m a woman, and that’s the perspective that feels like home,” says the director when asked about why she decided to focus on two young women. “And, to be honest, I think women live more interesting lives [laughs]. We have it harder, but our lives are very rich and unexamined still. We’ve had wonderful films and novels in the past decades dealing with the interior lives of women, but I still feel like there is still so much that is left unexplored and so many interesting characters that still haven’t been able to speak to the audience. So someone else can make a film about the male loneliness epidemic, I’m all for it, but it’s not going to be me [laughs].”

	Menart always knew her film would hinge on the casting of the two main actors. “I wanted actors from Slovenia because language is very important to me, and that meant our pool of actors was not huge,” she notes. “I still wanted to do open auditions, so I urged everyone and everyone’s friends to send in self-tapes to see what we would get.”

	Funnily enough, the two stars sent in tapes for the opposite characters. This, the director says, made her realize that “they each brought in an aspect of their personality that maybe would be missing in the script for the character.” After casting was completed, Menart spent a year working with the actors on developing their characters and adjusting the script accordingly. 
	

	Another key aspect of the production was finding the perfect location for Alja’s home, which ended up being the small German seaside town of Heringsdorf. “I was really attracted to this flat landscape, which is something we don’t really have where I am from,” says the director. “I also wanted to have a big contrast from where Maruša comes from, which is all very steep and claustrophobic. I wanted to have this feeling that when she arrives at this other location, everything opens a bit.”

	“It was a bit of a challenge because it is a tourist town that doesn’t have the infrastructure to support the making of a feature,” she adds. “There was no space to park trucks, so we had to be very agile and work with smaller vans and not a lot of equipment, very minimal lights. But it actually suited me very well. It’s a small story and very intimate, so I wanted to be flexible and I couldn’t plan everything ahead.”

	Speaking of intimacy, Menart wanted to work with a cinematographer with a documentary background, who “would approach this shoot as more of ‘let’s catch the actors doing something’ instead of ‘let’s make the actors do something.’” When she met Dutch cinematographer Roy van Egmond through a producer friend, she “connected immediately.” “It was important for us to have this great conversation between the camera and the actors so that the camera would enter the intimacy of this very close relationship. We felt we needed to have this little cocoon of people who really understood one another.” 

	As for having the world premiere of the film in Sarajevo, Menart says she is “really happy” to be back at the festival after presenting “Everything That’s Wrong With You” as part of CineLink, Sarajevo’s industry arm. “The festival is like a joyful high school reunion of the whole region, and they were so supportive of the film while we were making it. It feels perfect.”

	“Everything That’s Wrong With You” is produced by Slovenia’s Vertigo in co-production with Germany’s Chromosom Film, Tidewater Pictures, Serbia’s Living Pictures and RTV Slovenija. It is supported by the Slovenian Film Centre, MV Filmförderung, Film Center Serbia, the Ministry of Culture of the Republic of Serbia, Creative Europe MEDIA, the Ministry of Public Administration of the Republic of Slovenia, and Re-Act Co-Development Funding. In collaboration with Film Studio Viba Film.

schema.headline: Urša Menart Recalls Finding Inspiration on Influencers’ Fake Tragic Life Stories for Intimate Dramedy ‘Everything That’s Wrong With You’

title: ‘Nowhere to Lay My Eyes’ Review: Kim Minhee Once More Gives a Melancholy Masterclass in a Hong Sangsoo Miniature
description: The death-and-taxes certainty of Hong Sangsoo‘s filmography — comparable to Woody Allen’s prime career run in its regularity, consistency and recurr
body:
The death-and-taxes certainty of Hong Sangsoo‘s filmography — comparable to Woody Allen’s prime career run in its regularity, consistency and recurrence of ideas and actors across a gently varying tonal spectrum — has lately been infused with some mild unpredictability. Earlier this year, his Berlinale premiere “The Day She Returns” continued an occasional experimental jag in which story and imagery alike are left out of focus; the forbidding title “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes” might hint at more of the same. Instead, the director’s 35th feature is as classically and welcomingly Hong as it gets: a brief, bittersweet comedy of familial distance and personal drift, crisply and candidly shot, and built around a marvelous performance of quiet, more-than-meets-the-eye feeling by his partner and longtime muse Kim Minhee. 
	

	That last asset hasn’t been a given of late: Though the “Handmaiden” star has been exclusively a member of Hong’s company since 2017, she has served a number of Hong’s films in supporting or even off-camera roles. “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes” is Kim’s most rewarding showcase in several years, very much taking its atmospheric cues from her porous, watchful melancholy as a performer, while the presence of other Hong regulars — notably the trusty Kwon Haehyo, again in something of a proxy role for the auteur himself — in the tight ensemble gives the film a comforting gang’s-all-here air, along with a dry seam of humor. 


	Still, there are strains of deeper sadness and discomfort here, largely in the passive-aggressive tension between Kim’s character and her onscreen mother (superbly played by a new recuit, veteran TV star Choi Myeonggil). The film is slim — just 72 minutes — but it sticks. Following it Locarno competition premiere, “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes” will next play in the main slate of the New York Film Festival alongside “The Day She Returns.” Both will be released in North America by Hong’s regular distributor The Cinema Guild; at this point the director may not be minting that many arthouse converts, but the new film will be warmly embraced by the faithful.
	

	By day, Sanghee (Kim) works for an importer of foreign snack products, but she moonlights as an experimental filmmaker, posting her poetically ruminative shorts on YouTube. This life balance between art and commerce suits her fine, though it’s swiftly picked apart by her mother (Choi), who sees little value in her daughter’s job or her hobby. She could play nicer, considering the two women haven’t seen each other in a decade: Having been mostly raised by her grandparents after her parents’ divorce, Sanghee feels no great kinship with her mom, but hopes a weekend visit to the latter’s new home on the remote, picturesque Jeju Island might rebuild some bridges.

	Traveling from Seoul, Sanghee is accompanied by her brother (Shin Seokho), whom her mother treats with markedly more respect. Her mother, meanwhile, is backed up by her second husband (Kwon), a mild-mannered documentary filmmaker whose profession gives his wife yet more ammunition in her smiling disparagement of Sanghee. A restaurant owner who has recently renovated a holiday rental cottage adjoining her property, the older woman has a metric for personal success that doesn’t prioritize personal contentment. Sanghee does have support, however, from her younger stepsister (Park Miso), a shy aspiring artist who admires both her films and her principles; if only Sanghee liked her more.

	Over two days of meals, walks and (this being a typical Hong work) slightly excessive drinking, these awkwardly assembled relatives spar softly without (this being a typical Hong work) making much drama of it. The substance here is in the film’s pointed observation of their various coping strategies, blind spots and small, satisfying moments of release. The running conversation between them roves from European furniture quality to opposing modes of documentary practice — Sanghee, like Hong, is prolific and off-the-cuff in her filming, while her stepfather patiently nurtures longterm projects — to, in a rare topical diversion for the filmmaker, the war in Gaza.

	Beneath it all, of course, what they’re really talking about is their own respective flavors of loneliness and regret and occasional bliss; “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes” takes interest and even pleasure in all of these, as well as in the throwaway highlights — a great noodle soup, a perfect accidental pratfall —  of even the most fraught day. Minhee’s economical performance is beautifully attuned to those alternately profound and superficial concerns, as her face works hard to contain Sanghee’s simultaneous amusement and disappointment at this pleasant, awful weekend, while her sporadic voiceover betrays the more lyrically wounded woman within. That narration is a less usual Hong feature, but a successful one: Even on his most quintessential form, the director can find small, sly ways to surprise us.

schema.headline: ‘Nowhere to Lay My Eyes’ Review: Kim Minhee Once More Gives a Melancholy Masterclass in a Hong Sangsoo Miniature

title: ‘A Chocolate Christmas,’ a Brazilian Holiday Romantic Drama, Set to Shoot in Gramado and New York From December
description: GRAMADO, Brazil — Vet Brazilian helmer-producer Paulo Nascimento will lense “A Chocolate Christmas,” a Portuguese-language holiday-themed feature fi
body:
GRAMADO, Brazil — Vet Brazilian helmer-producer Paulo Nascimento will lense “A Chocolate Christmas,” a Portuguese-language holiday-themed feature film in the mountain resort of Gramado, in southern Brazil, and New York City, he told Variety. 

	The film will shoot over December and January. Nascimento is set announce the film project t his panel on Sunday at the Gramado Film Festival.


	“A Chocolate Christmas” weighs in as a romantic drama set mainly during Natal Luz de Gramado, recognized by Guinness as the world’s longest Christmas festival. 
	

	The pic is produced by Nascimento’s Accorde Filmes and H2O Films, with co-production from NYC-based indie production company Rose Pictures. H2O, one of the leading independent distributors in Brazil, is to open the pic in local theaters over the 2027 Christmas season.

	Nascimento said he will shoot the feature during one week in NYC in December 2026 and over four weeks in Gramado in January 2027, including exteriors set in Natal Luz de Gramado. The festivity includes Christmas parades with floats, performers and characters, an open-air show staged over water with music, fireworks and special effects, concerts with the Gramado Symphony Orchestra and an immersive performance combining technology, visual effects and illuminated costumes.

	“From a producer’s perspective, Natal Luz has a production value that not even a major Netflix production could provide. We will have access to all of the event’s activities and incorporate them into the film. In other words, we will have the scale of a major production without the corresponding costs,” Nascimento told Variety.
	

	The story follows Linda, a 17-year-old teenager who, after having her heart broken by her boyfriend, leaves her family in Gramado to study in the U.S. 10 years later, now recognized in the U.S. as a talented chocolatier and preparing to open her first chocolate shop in Manhattan, she is forced to return to Brazil after her father suffers a heart attack. Back in her hometown and involved once again with her family’s chocolate business, Linda reunites with her former boyfriend and, amid the traditions of Christmas in Gramado, rediscovers the possibility of opening her heart to love.

	Nascimento said he has directed 17 films in his career, including political drama “In Your Name,” winner of four Kikito prizes at the Gramado Fest 2009, and “Westend of the World,” a co-production with Argentina starring Cesar Troncoso as a veteran of the Falklands War.

	His most recent features are “13 Souls,” a supernatural possession horror movie distributed online in the U.K. in May via Seven Tales and Trinity Content Partners, and the still unreleased “The Taxidermist.”

	“I have always made political dramas, and now I’m making genre films: a horror film, a melodrama and a Christmas movie. Cinema has shifted toward niche films,” Nascimento observed.

schema.headline: ‘A Chocolate Christmas,’ a Brazilian Holiday Romantic Drama, Set to Shoot in Gramado and New York From December

title: Zee Entertainment Wins Interim Relief to Proceed With $330 Million Capital Raise Despite Indian Regulator’s Market Ban
description: India’s Securities Appellate Tribunal has granted media giant Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. interim relief in its dispute with the country’s se
body:
India’s Securities Appellate Tribunal has granted media giant Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. interim relief in its dispute with the country’s securities regulator, allowing the company to proceed with the promoter fund infusion at the center of last month’s shareholder vote despite an ongoing market ban — on the condition that Zee first deposits the penalty the regulator imposed on it. 

	The tribunal reserved judgment on the broader stay sought by Zee and its top management against the market-access restrictions themselves, meaning the underlying ban remains in place for now. The stock rose more than 5% on the news.
	

	Earlier, shareholders of Indian media giant Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. had approved a promoter group fund infusion worth INR3143.5 crore ($330 million) and a new employee stock option plan at an extraordinary general meeting, a day before India’s securities regulator barred the company and two of its top executives from the market.


	The Mumbai-headquartered media and technology company said its shareholders backed a preferential issue of 249,485,563 warrants to a promoter group entity, priced at INR126 ($1.32) each. A warrant gives its holder the right to convert it into a company share at a later date, at a price fixed now. Once exercised, the promoters’ stake will grow to 23.79% of the company.

	Shareholders also cleared the “Truly Yours” employee stock option plan, under which 37,422,835 stock options with a face value of INR1 ($0.01) each will be granted to eligible employees of Zee and its subsidiaries, in one or more tranches.
	

	R. Gopalan, chair of Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd., thanked shareholders for their support. “This approval is a clear reflection of the shareholders’ belief in the Company and its management,” Gopalan said. “The board firmly believes that robust growth capital coupled with enhanced promoter alignment, will serve as key enablers in ensuring long-term profitability in a dynamic business environment.”

	A day after the shareholder vote, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) – the country’s capital markets watchdog – issued an order barring Zee from the securities market for two months and barring chair emeritus Subhash Chandra and managing director and CEO Punit Goenka from the market for 12 months each. SEBI also imposed penalties totaling INR1.48 crore ($155,000), split between INR30 lakh ($31,000) on Zee, INR58 lakh ($61,000) on Goenka and INR60 lakh ($63,000) on Chandra.

	The order concerns the pledge of a Zee-owned property in Hyderabad, used in December 2018 to secure INR726 crore ($76.1 million) in loans for four entities linked to Essel Group, the promoter group associated with Chandra and Goenka. SEBI found the pledge was never disclosed to or approved by Zee’s board or audit committee, and determined that Chandra and Goenka had used the company’s asset to shield borrowings tied to their own family-controlled entities.

	A company spokesperson said Zee was reviewing the order with legal counsel and did not expect it to affect the fund-raising exercise. “The company would like to clarify that pursuant to the regulatory approvals received from the stock exchanges and from its esteemed shareholders at the Extraordinary General Meeting conducted on 31st July 2026, it will further take all required steps to successfully complete the fund-raising exercise, which is aimed at strengthening its financial foundation, and will also continue to work towards creating value for its stakeholders,” the spokesperson said.

	The order is the latest in a long-running SEBI probe into Zee’s promoters. The regulator first barred Goenka and Chandra from holding managerial or directorial roles at listed companies in June 2023, over allegations of fund diversion. The Securities Appellate Tribunal set aside that order that October, but the scrutiny continued to shadow Zee’s proposed $10 billion merger with Sony Pictures Networks India, which collapsed in January 2024. Chandra later accused SEBI’s then-chair of scuttling the merger.
	

	In the two years since, Zee has cut roughly 15% of its workforce and expanded into sports broadcasting, striking a deal with FIFA in June for Indian broadcast and streaming rights to the 2026 and 2030 World Cups and 37 other tournaments through 2034.

	The newly approved capital is earmarked for that broader push, with the company directing the funds toward sports, acquisitions, digital content, artificial intelligence and microdrama through fiscal 2029, with sports receiving the largest share.

schema.headline: Zee Entertainment Wins Interim Relief to Proceed With $330 Million Capital Raise Despite Indian Regulator’s Market Ban

title: Florin Şerban’s ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ Wins Golden Leopard at Locarno, as Monica Bellucci and Kim Minhee Take Acting Awards
description: Romanian director Florin Şerban’s “You Don’t Belong Here,” a somber study of anti-Roma racism in the country, has taken the Golden Lion for best fil
body:
Romanian director Florin Şerban’s “You Don’t Belong Here,” a somber study of anti-Roma racism in the country, has taken the Golden Lion for best film in the International Competition at the Locarno Film Festival, along with a special mention for its young star Teodor Butănescu. The film emerged victorious in a lineup of 17 features at the Swiss fest, including new works by auteurs including Hong Sangsoo, Denis Côté, Ann Oren and Nelson Yeo. It was awarded by a jury headed by Belgian filmmaker Fabrice Du Welz; his fellow jurors included actors Paulina Garcia and Lolita Chammah, producer Marco Alessi and Arte France Cinéma executive director Olivier Père.
	

	“You Don’t Belong Here” reps a return to international festival prominence for Şerban, whose 2010 debut feature “If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle” won the Grand Prix in the Berlinale competition, but whose subsequent features have had less impact. The story of a respected doctor discovering that his son has committed a racially motivated murder, his latest was a consensus choice across the festival, also taking the festival’s Junior Jury and Europa Cinemas Label honors. Variety critic Jay Weissberg, however, was less impressed, declaring in a mostly negative review that the film “opens with great promise and finishes with a stupefyingly misguided coda.”


	Veteran Korean auteur Hong didn’t leave Locarno empty-handed. Eleven years after his signature comedy “Right Now, Wrong Then” won the Golden Leopard, he was named Best Director for his 35th feature “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes,” a bittersweet family-reunion study that this critic praised for being “as classically and welcomingly Hong as it gets.” 
	

	The director’s partner and muse Kim Minhee was another repeat winner, taking the gender-neutral Best Performance award for her quietly affecting turn as an amateur filmmaker spending an awkward weekend with her estranged mother — just two years after taking the same prize in Locarno for Hong’s “By the Stream.” Kim shared the honor with Italian icon Monica Bellucci for her supporting role in Giovanni Tortorici’s coming-of-age tale “Ketticè” — a choice more endorsed by Weissberg, whose review celebrated the star as having “few equals in her ability to project self-aware drama queen with just the right dose of camp icon.” 

	Rounding out the International Competition awards, Brazilian directors Matheus Farias and Enock Carvalho won the Special Jury Prize for their queer erotic thriller “The Riverbank,” which traces the bond between a cleaner and a fisherman on the mangrove-strewn fringes of Recife. Canadian actor Xavier Bergeron also landed a special mention for his performance in Côté’s “Nobody’s Violence.” 

	Somewhat surprisingly overlooked by the jury, however, was festival buzz title “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” a striking portrait of a transgender marriage amid the upheaval of the war in Ukraine from German director Isabelle Stever; it will have its North American premiere in the main slate of the New York Film Festival next month.

	Outside the main competition, Argentine-American photographer Alessandra Sanguinetti’s directorial debut “The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer” was the big winner, taking the top prize in the festival’s secondary Filmmakers of the Present competition, as well as the separately juried award for Best First Feature. 

	A documentary filmed over the course of 25 years, “Summer” follows two closely bonded female cousins in Argentina’s rural Pampas region from childhood to womanhood, and was one of the festival’s word-of-mouth critical sensations; it will be distributed by Mubi in North America and the U.K. Another freshman helmer, British artist Beatrice Gibson, was named Best Emerging Director by the Filmmakers of the Present jury for her BBC-backed hybrid doc “At Night.”

	The 79th Locarno Film Festival will close tonight with a gala screening of French director Marc Fitoussi’s meta film-industry comedy “All About Corinne,” starring Isabelle Huppert and Sandrine Kiberlain.
	

	Full list of winners below:

	Golden Leopard for Best Film: “You Don’t Belong Here,” Florin ȘerbanSpecial Jury Prize: “The Riverbank,” Matheus Farias, Enock CarvalhoBest Direction: Hong Sangsoo, “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes”Best Performance: Kim Minhee, “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes”; Monica Bellucci, “Ketticè”Special Mention for Performance: Xavier Bergeron, “Nobody’s Violence”; Teodor Butănescu, “You Don’t Belong Here”

title: Diego Luna, Nicolas Pereda and Rodrigo Plá Set for Competition at Mexico’s Morelia Film Festival
description: A-list festival acclaimed pics from some of Mexico’s most celebrated talent, many of them female and first-timers, make up this year’s line-up at th
body:
A-list festival acclaimed pics from some of Mexico’s most celebrated talent, many of them female and first-timers, make up this year’s line-up at the Morelia Film Festival (FICM).

	Running October 16-25, the 24th FICM edition features such luminaries as actor-producer Diego Luna (“Andor”) in his fifth outing as a director in “Ashes,” which world premiered in Cannes and was picked up by Netflix for Latin America, Spain and Portugal. It’s co-produced by Animal de Luz, run by Inna Payan whose directorial debut “Liliana’s Invincible Summer” (co-helmed with Samuel Kishi) will stream on Netflix.
	

	Also leading the pack of a dozen fiction features in competition for Morelia’s top Ojo Award, is Nicolas Pereda’s wry ‘Everything Else is Noise.” (“Lo demás es ruido”), acquired ahead of its debuts at the Toronto Film Festival (TIFF) and the New York Film Festival (NYFF) by U.S.-based distributor Pragda; Rodrigo Plá’s “The Newcomers” (“Los Nuevos”), a Patra Spanou pick-up soon after its world premiere at Locarno’s Kids Screenings and Fernanda Tovar’s feature debut “Sad Girlz,” snagged by Alpha Violet before its Berlinale debut.


	A total of 96 feature-length and short films, helmed by filmmakers from 17 states across Mexico, will compete in their respective sections for El Ojo, a sculpture created by Michoacán artist Javier Marín, along with cash and in-kind awards.

	Dovetailing with the festival’s aim for diversity and inclusion, women directed 40% of the pics in the Official Selection, while some competing films were directed by filmmakers from Indigenous communities.
	

	“This has been one of the most fruitful years for the Mexican Feature Film section, which is a great source of pride for the festival. Interestingly, unlike in recent years, when we received between 80 and 100 fiction features, this year we received just 68. Yet the quality of those films made the final selection particularly challenging. We initially planned to select eight titles, but the exceptional quality and sensitivity of the work ultimately led us to expand the lineup to 12,” said Rafael Aviña, a member of the FICM selection committee.

	This year’s fiction lineup sees some overriding themes. Several of the pics look back at Mexico in the 1990s, while others follow teenagers navigating contemporary issues in an increasingly complicated society where their horizons feel narrower than ever. The selection also includes more experimental films, as well as stories centered on childhood – an unusual focus to date for Mexican feature filmmaking.

	Senior programmer and documentary programming coordinator Chloë Roddick also sees a robust year for Mexican documentaries. “In both [feature and shorts] sections, the real challenge for us this year was to narrow the selection down (12 titles in feature doc; 11 in shorts). The final selection reflects both the breadth of talent currently working on the documentary scene, as well as a plurality of stories, a strong interest in challenging structure and form and a diverse mix of voices – from first-time to more established filmmakers.”

	“As in previous years we saw strong feature and short film representation from Mexico´s Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities and the final selection includes three films by Indigenous filmmakers: Ramon Llaven´s ‘El baile de las ánimas’ and the short films ‘Ni racaladxe’ ‘(a co-direction from Zapotec director Alma Yoari Cizana Lopez) and Hñähñu filmmaker Sara Stephany Padilla´s ‘Mascaras del tiempo.’”

	“In the feature selection, films like Efrain Mojica and Rebecca Zweig´s Michoacán-set ‘Jarpieo’ premieres in Morelia after a healthy international festival run that included Sundance, Berlinale, CPH:Dox and True/False. Dano Garcia´s bold and genre-defying exploration of queer identity, ‘Mickey,’ premiered at SXSW, as did Otilia Padua Portillo´s immersive sci-fi portrait of Indigenous mushroom scientists, ‘Las hijas del bosque.’ First-time filmmaker Colette Ghunim´s nuanced and intimate portrait of her Mexican/Palestinian roots, ‘Traces of Home,’ exec produced by Melissa Barrera and John Leguizamo, bowed at DOC NYC.“
	

	The documentary selection includes six more first features: Francisco Ohem’s Balkans-set “Los mariachis perdidos”; Pablo Vaca’s coming-of-age observational drama (with a twist) “Forensita”; ‘Yatra,’ Alejandro Rugama´s deeply personal exploration of sickness and isolation; Indigenous Chiapas-born filmmaker Ramon Llaven’s “El baile de las ánimas”; Vania Carolina Quevedo´s video-essay and ode to her baby daughter, “Mi sangre es petroleo” and Michoacán-born Mariano Renteria’s architectural opera ‘Odisea Nacional,’ which also participated in Morelia’s works-in-progress section, Impulso Morelia, in 2025.

	Winning short films in the Fiction, Animation and Documentary categories, along with the Mexican Documentary Feature winner, will be eligible to vie for an Academy Award nomination.

	Additionally, a selection of short films from this year’s crop will be invited to screen out of competition during the Cannes Festival’s Critics’ Week in 2027.

	Fiction Features in Competition

	“Against Nature” (“Contra la naturaleza”), Axel Bertha“A Lifetime” (“Toda una vida”), Ariel Gutiérrez“Ashes” (“Ceniza en la boca”), Diego Luna“Everything Else is Noise” (“Lo demás es ruido”), Nicolás Pereda“The Garden We Dreamed” (“El jardín que soñamos”), Joaquín del Paso“The Huntress” (“La cazadora”), Suzanne Andrews Correa“The Newcomers” (“Los nuevos”), Rodrigo Plá“The Nine Days of Poncho” (“Los días de Poncho”), Faustino Alanís“Nosotros” (“Nosotros”), Joaquín Ruano“Salón de Belleza” (“Salón de belleza”), Nathalia Acevedo“Sad Girlz” (“Chicas tristes”), Fernanda Tovar“Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building” (“6 meses en el edificio rosa con azul”), Bruno Santamaría Razo

	Documentaries

	“Daughters of the Forest” (“Hijas del bosque”), Otilia Portillo Padua“Dear Fátima” (“Querida Fátima”), Lorena Gutiérrez, Rodrigo Reyes, Jesús Quintana“Jaripeo” (“Jaripeo”), Efraín Mojica, Rebecca Zweig“Lost Mariachis” (“Los mariachis perdidos”), Francisco Ohem“Mickey” (“Mickey”), Dano García“My Blood Is Oil” (“Mi sangre es petróleo”), Vania Carolina Quevedo“National Odyssey” (“Odisea nacional”), Mariano Rentería“Reportage” (“Reportaje”), Nicolás Gutiérrez“The Dance of the Souls” (“El baile de las ánimas”), Ramón Llaven“The Little Forensic” (“Forensita”), Pablo Vaca“Traces of Home” (“Traces of Home”), Colette Ghunim“Yātrā” (“yātrā”), Alejandro Rugama

            Ryan was 40.

title: Cambridge University Professor Jason Arday Found Dead Amid Plagiarism Scandal
description:
Ex-Cambridge Professor
                          Jason Arday Found Dead In London ...
body:
Ex-Cambridge Professor
                          Jason Arday Found Dead In London ...
                          After Being Accused Of Plagiarism
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 15, 2026
                            5:23 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jason Arday, the Cambridge professor who resigned after being accused of plagiarism, has died, according to the university.
      
    
            In a statement Friday, Deborah Prentice, the Vice-Chancellor Professor at the University of Cambridge, confirmed Arday's death, saying "we are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news" and "our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Metropolitan Police in London said officers responded to a man's home Friday afternoon after receiving a report that he was found unresponsive. Police declared the man dead at the scene and notified his next of kin without releasing Arday's name publicly.
      

            Investigators are calling the death "unexpected" but not suspicious, and are trying to determine how he died.
      
    
            In 2023, Arday was hired at Cambridge as the youngest Black professor teaching sociology of education. He was considered an academic scholar who focused on race and inequality. But more recently, Arday was hit with allegations of plagiarism in his work at the university and other projects. 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            At first, Cambridge pledged its support to Arday, but then the Times of London published a story examining Arday’s 2015 Ph.D. thesis, which contained  “identical or near-identical” passages found in a paper penned by a different researcher at an earlier date.
      
    
            The British press also raised doubts about Arday's assertions that he collected $7.4 million in charity money by winning athletic competitions, claiming at one point he ran 30 marathons in 35 days.
      
    
            On August 5, Cambridge launched an investigation into Arday's "qualifications and honorary appointments," leading to his resignation.
      
    
            Arday was 41.
      
    
            RIP

body:
Da'Vine Joy Randolph
                          Sues Landlord Over $17k a Month Rental Claiming Pest and Plumbing Issues
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 15, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Da’Vine Joy Randolph is dragging her landlord to court … claiming she rented a luxury home for $17K a month … only to have to deal with pests and plumbing issues ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            The Oscar-winning actress is suing a leasing company, 421 NRD LLC, claiming its $5+ million rental turned into a nightmare with a whole host of problems.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Da’Vine said she leased a high-end 5-bedroom, 6-bathroom, 4,452-square-foot home in Los Angeles for $17,000 per month in September 2024.
      

            She said the company promised the home was in good condition ... but says she moved in and had to deal with water issues, pest conditions, door and window failures, defective locks, plumbing conditions, inconsistent water pressure, and safety concerns.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Da’Vine claims that when she raised the issues, the landlord made insufficient fixes and eventually told her she could move out if she was unhappy.
      
    
            The actress is suing for breach of the lease and bunch of other things.  She's seeking unspecified damages and wants to be reimbursed for her out-of-pocket expenses like hotels she had to stay in during repairs and pest control.
